title: Normalizer and centralizer of a torus have the same identity component
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Use reductivity, maximal tori, and scheme-theoretic centralizer points as in [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $G$ be smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], and let $S\subseteq G$ be any torus. Define $N_G(S)(A)$ to be the elements of $G(A)$ whose conjugation preserves $S_{A\prime}$ as a subgroup functor after every commutative $A$-algebra extension $A\prime$. Then $N_G(S)$ and $C_G(S)$ are represented by smooth closed subgroup schemes of finite type and $$N_G(S)^\circ=C_G(S)^\circ.$$ The superscript $\circ$ denotes the connected component of the identity. In particular $N_G(S)(F)/C_G(S)(F)$ is a finite group.

source.place: Corollary 12.40, printed p.244 (same identity component); Corollary 13.10, printed p.257 (smooth normalizer and centralizer); Corollary 13.11, printed p.257 (geometric-point descriptions). Finiteness follows from the finitely many components of a finite-type scheme.

proof.text: Let $f:S\times_FG\to G$ be $f(s,g)=gsg^{-1}$. Apply [lem-sfb-constant-source-closed-factorization-locus] with source $S$, parameter scheme $G$, target $G$, and closed subscheme $S\hookrightarrow G$. The separatedness hypotheses hold by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-source-morphism-separated], since both schemes are affine. This gives a closed subscheme $L\subseteq G$ whose $A$-points are exactly those $g$ for which conjugation sends $S_A$ into $S_A$. This is equivalent to $g_{A'}S(A')g_{A'}^{-1}\subseteq S(A')$ for every $A$-algebra $A'$: the forward implication follows by evaluating the factorization; for the converse, test with the coordinate algebra of $S_A$ and its universal point. The defining ideal of $S_A$ then pulls back to zero, giving the factorization by the affine quotient-ring criterion in [def-weil-closed-immersion]. Pull back $L$ by inversion and intersect with $L$, obtaining $N=L\times_G\operatorname{inv}^{-1}(L)$. The fibre-product property [def-pc-fibre-product] and [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-base-change] give this intersection. Explicitly, if $G=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $L$ is cut out by $I\subseteq B$, the intersection is cut out by $I+\operatorname{inv}^*I$, so it is closed in $G$. Its test condition is the preceding inclusion for both $g$ and $g^{-1}$, which is precisely equality $gS_Ag^{-1}=S_A$. Thus $N$ represents the normalizer functor $N_G(S)$ defined in the statement.

source.place: Proposition 1.79 and Proposition 1.83, printed pp.30--31; the closed-family construction is Theorem 1.105, pp.37--38.

proof.text: The identity preserves $S$; if $g$ and $h$ preserve $S$ after every algebra extension, then $gh$ does, because $(gh)s(gh)^{-1}=g(hsh^{-1})g^{-1}$; the inverse condition is built into $N$. Hence $N(A)$ is a subgroup of $G(A)$ naturally in $A$, so [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] makes $N$ a closed subgroup scheme. By [def-weil-closed-immersion], its coordinate ring is a quotient of the finitely generated $F$-algebra of $G$. The images of a finite generating set still generate the quotient, so $N$ is affine of finite type. By [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], applied over the algebraically closed field $F$ to the given smooth connected $G$ and the torus $S$, $C=C_G(S)$ is a smooth closed subgroup scheme of $G$. It too is affine of finite type by the same quotient argument. Every point centralizing $S$ preserves $S$, so $C\subseteq N$ on all test algebras.

source.place: Proposition 1.83, pp.31--32; Corollary 13.10, p.257 (only its centralizer assertion is used here).

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates] to $N$ and $C$, writing $N^\circ,C^\circ$ for their identity components with their open subscheme structures. They are connected open-and-closed subgroup schemes. In particular $N^\circ$ is affine of finite type, being closed in the affine finite-type scheme $N$. Conjugation restricts to a morphism $\phi:N^\circ\times_FS\to S$: the universal property defining $L$ gives the factorization, and conjugation by the inverse gives its inverse in the $S$ variable. For each algebra and parameter point this is a group homomorphism, by the identity $g(s_1s_2)g^{-1}=(gs_1g^{-1})(gs_2g^{-1})$. Choose the given splitting $S\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. The Laurent monomials $t_1^{m_1}\cdots t_r^{m_r}$ identify its coordinate Hopf algebra with $F[\mathbf Z^r]$: multiplication adds exponent vectors, comultiplication repeats the monomial in both factors, and the counit evaluates it at $1$. Thus [lem-sfb-diagonalizable-hom-family-rigidity] applies with $X=N^\circ$, $D_1=D_2=S$, and $x_0=e$. It requires no smoothness or reducedness of $X$. It gives $\phi(g,s)=\phi(e,s)=s$ on every algebra. Consequently $N^\circ\subseteq C$ as subgroup schemes, including their possibly nonreduced structures.

source.place: Theorem 12.36 and proof of Corollary 12.40, printed pp.243--244.

proof.text: Since the connected scheme $C^\circ$ maps into $N$ and contains its identity, its image lies in the identity component of $N$; [lem-weil-pbc-morphism-factors-through-open-subscheme] factors $C^\circ\to N$ through the open subscheme $N^\circ$. Conversely, the inclusion $N^\circ\subseteq C$ from Step 3 has connected image containing the identity, so its image lies in $C^\circ$, and the same open-factorization statement factors it through $C^\circ$. These two maps compose to the identity: after their subgroup inclusions in $G$, both composites are the original inclusions, which are injective on every algebra's points. Hence $N^\circ=C^\circ$ as subgroup schemes of $G$, with their open subscheme structures. The inclusions and open structures used here are precisely those supplied by [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates].

source.place: Corollary 12.40, p.244; identity-component inclusions and their induced scheme structures.

proof.text: By [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes], the open subscheme $C^\circ$ of the smooth scheme $C$ is smooth. The equality in Step 4 therefore makes $N^\circ$ smooth. By [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], every connected component $D$ of $N$ has its open subscheme structure and is isomorphic over $F$ to $N^\circ$ by translation by some $n_D\in N(F)$. Smoothness is unchanged under such an isomorphism by clause (c) of [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-restrict-open-subschemes]. The components cover $N$, so [lem-weil-pbc-smooth-local-on-source] makes $N$ smooth. This proves smoothness without having assumed it when applying rigidity.

source.place: Corollary 13.10, printed p.257: deduce normalizer smoothness from its identity component and translation.

proof.text: The centralizer is normal in $N$: for $n\in N(A)$, $c\in C(A)$ and $s\in S(A')$ after any $A$-algebra extension, put $t=n^{-1}sn\in S(A')$. Then $(ncn^{-1})s=nctn^{-1}=ntcn^{-1}=s(ncn^{-1})$. Thus $ncn^{-1}\in C(A)$, and in particular $N(F)/C(F)$ is a group. There are only finitely many connected components of $N$ by [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates]; choose its representatives $n_D$ from that same statement. Every $n\in N(F)$ in component $D$ has $n_D^{-1}n\in N^\circ(F)=C^\circ(F)\subseteq C(F)$. Therefore every coset of $C(F)$ is represented by one of the finitely many $n_D$, and the quotient group is finite.

source.place: Corollary 12.40, p.244, and Proposition 1.34/Corollary 1.35, printed pp.16--17, for the finite component/coset argument.

proof_origin.place: Propositions 1.79 and 1.83, Theorem 12.36, Corollaries 12.40 and 13.10; finite components from Proposition 1.34 and Corollary 1.35.

lean.statement: theorem torus_normalizer_centralizer_components (F : Type u) [Field F] [IsAlgClosed F] (G S : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) [IsAffine G.X.left] [LocallyOfFiniteType G.X.hom] [QuasiCompact G.X.hom] [Smooth G.X.hom] [ConnectedSpace G.X.left] (i : S ⟶ G) [IsClosedSubgroupScheme i.hom.hom] (hS : ∃ r : ℕ, Nonempty (S ≅ MultiplicativeType.splitTorus F r)) : ∃ (N C : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (iN : N ⟶ G) (iC : C ⟶ G), IsClosedSubgroupScheme iN.hom.hom ∧ IsClosedSubgroupScheme iC.hom.hom ∧ IsAffine N.X.left ∧ IsAffine C.X.left ∧ ∃ (_ : LocallyOfFiniteType N.X.hom) (_ : QuasiCompact N.X.hom) (_ : LocallyOfFiniteType C.X.hom) (_ : QuasiCompact C.X.hom), Smooth N.X.hom ∧ Smooth C.X.hom ∧ (∀ (A : Type u) [CommRing A] [Algebra F A], Set.range (fun n : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F A ⟶ N.X ↦ n ≫ iN.hom.hom) = {g : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F A ⟶ G.X | ∀ (B : Type u) [CommRing B] [Algebra F B] (f : A →ₐ[F] B), (fun s : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F B ⟶ G.X ↦ (StandardGroupSchemes.map F f ≫ g) * s * (StandardGroupSchemes.map F f ≫ g)⁻¹) '' Set.range (fun s : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F B ⟶ S.X ↦ s ≫ i.hom.hom) = Set.range (fun s : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F B ⟶ S.X ↦ s ≫ i.hom.hom)}) ∧ (∀ (A : Type u) [CommRing A] [Algebra F A], Set.range (fun c : StandardGroupSchemes.affine F A ⟶ C.X ↦ c ≫ iC.hom.hom) = ReductiveTorusCentralizer.centralizerPoints i A) ∧ (∃ e : GrpObj.identityComponent N.X ≅ GrpObj.identityComponent C.X, e.hom ≫ GrpObj.identityComponentι C.X ≫ iC.hom.hom = GrpObj.identityComponentι N.X ≫ iN.hom.hom) ∧ ∃ j : C ⟶ N, j ≫ iN = iC ∧ IsNormalSubgroupScheme j.hom.hom ∧ Finite ((𝟙_ (Over (Spec (.of F))) ⟶ N.X) ⧸ (IsMonHom.monoidHom j.hom.hom (𝟙_ (Over (Spec (.of F))))).range)
